title: VII. The First And Rightful Lover
paragraphs: With his long, rapid strides, Mitya walked straight up to the table.

“Gentlemen,” he said loudly, almost shouting, yet stammering on every word, “I—I'm fine! Don't be afraid!” he exclaimed. “There's nothing the matter with me,” he said, turning suddenly to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand tightly. “I—I'm coming too. I'll stay until morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Just until morning, for the last time, in this same room?”
He finished by turning to the fat little man with the pipe, sitting on the sofa. The man removed his pipe from his lips with dignity and observed severely:
“_Panie_, we're here in private. There are other rooms.”
“Why, it's you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What are you doing?” Kalganov put in suddenly. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“Delighted to see you, dear—precious fellow, I always thought a lot of you,” Mitya responded joyfully and eagerly, at once reaching his hand across the table.
“Ouch! You squeeze so hard! You've nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

“He always squeezes like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile, suddenly convinced from Mitya's face that he wasn't going to make a scene. She was watching him with intense curiosity and still some unease. Something about him impressed her, and the last thing she'd expected was that he would walk in and speak like this at such a moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov ventured blandly on the left. Mitya rushed up to him too.

“Good evening. You're here too! How glad I am to find you here as well! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned back to the Polish gentleman with the pipe, evidently taking him for the most important person present.) “I flew here. I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room—where I too adored—my queen. Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly. “I flew here and swore—Oh, don't be afraid, it's my last night! Let's drink to our good understanding. The wine will be here any minute. I brought this with me.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of banknotes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a celebration, the way we had before. But the worm, the unnecessary worm, will crawl away, and there'll be no more of him. I'll mark my day of joy on my last night.”

He was almost choking. There was so much, so much he wanted to say, but only strange exclamations kept coming out. The Pole stared fixedly at him, at the bundle of notes in his hand, then looked at Grushenka, clearly puzzled.
“If my suverin lady is permitting—” he began.

“What does ‘suverin' mean? ‘Sovereign,' I suppose?” Grushenka interrupted. “I can't help laughing at the way you talk. Sit down, Mitya, what are you talking about? Don't frighten us, please. You won't frighten us, will you? If you won't, I'm glad to see you—”
“Me, frighten you?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won't get in your way!”

And suddenly he surprised them all—and no doubt himself too—by throwing himself into a chair and bursting into tears, turning his head away toward the opposite wall while his arms clutched the back of the chair tight, as though embracing it.

“Come on, what a fellow you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That's exactly how he comes to see me—he starts talking, and I can't make out what he means. He cried like that once before, and now he's crying again! It's shameful! What are you crying for? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added enigmatically, emphasizing each word with a touch of irritation.
“I—I'm not crying. Well, good evening!” He turned back in his chair at once and suddenly laughed—not his abrupt wooden laugh, but a long, quivering, almost inaudible nervous laugh.

“There you go again. Come, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka said coaxingly. “I'm very glad you've come, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I'm very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she said firmly, addressing the whole company, though her words were obviously meant for the man on the sofa. “I want it, I want it! And if he leaves, I'll leave too!” she added, her eyes flashing.
“Whatever my queen commands is law!” pronounced the Pole, gallantly kissing Grushenka's hand. “I beg you, _panie_, to join our company,” he added politely, turning to Mitya.
Mitya was about to jump up with the obvious intention of delivering another tirade, but the words wouldn't come.
“Let's drink, _panie_,” he blurted out instead of making a speech. Everyone laughed.

“Good heavens! I thought he was going to start again!” Grushenka exclaimed nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on insistently, “don't prance around, but it's nice that you brought champagne. I want some myself, and I can't stand liqueurs. And best of all, you've come yourself. We were terribly dull here. You've come for a spree again, I suppose? But put your money in your pocket. Where did you get so much?”

Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand the whole time, and every eye—especially the Poles'—was fixed on it. Embarrassed, he hurriedly stuffed them into his pocket. He flushed. At that moment the innkeeper brought in an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya snatched up the bottle, but he was so flustered he didn't know what to do with it. Kalganov took it from him and poured.

“Another! Another bottle!” Mitya called to the innkeeper, and, forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly invited to drink to their good understanding, he tossed back his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face suddenly changed. The solemn, tragic expression with which he'd entered vanished completely, and something childlike came into his face. He seemed to have turned suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked shyly and happily at everyone, with a continual nervous little laugh and the blissful expression of a dog who has done wrong, been punished, and forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything and was gazing around with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing constantly, and moved his chair close to hers. Gradually he had formed some idea of the two Poles, though he hadn't settled on any definite impression of them yet.

The Pole on the sofa struck him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and above all with his pipe. “Well, what of it? It's a good thing he's smoking a pipe,” he thought. The Pole's puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and two very thin, pointed, dyed, and impudent mustaches, hadn't yet raised the faintest doubt in Mitya. He wasn't even particularly struck by the Pole's absurd wig, made in Siberia, with silly love-locks combed forward over the temples. “I suppose it's all right since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other, younger Pole, who was staring insolently and defiantly at the company and listening to the conversation with silent contempt, still only impressed Mitya by his great height, which was in striking contrast to the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he'd be six foot three,” the thought flickered through Mitya's mind. It also occurred to him that this Pole must be the other one's friend—a kind of “bodyguard”—and that the big Pole was no doubt at the disposal of the little Pole with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly right and not to be questioned. In his mood of dog-like submissiveness, every feeling of rivalry had died away.

Grushenka's mood and the enigmatic tone of some of her words he completely failed to grasp. All he understood, with a thrilling heart, was that she was kind to him, that she had forgiven him, and had made him sit beside her. He was beside himself with delight, watching her sip her glass of champagne. But the silence in the company seemed to strike him, and he glanced around at everyone with expectant eyes.
“Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don't you start doing something?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He keeps talking nonsense, and we were all laughing at him,” Kalganov began suddenly, as though reading his thought, and pointed at Maximov.
Mitya immediately stared at Kalganov, then at Maximov.
“He's talking nonsense?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted at something. “Ha ha!”
“Yes. Would you believe it, he insists that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. That's absolute nonsense, isn't it?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, perfectly ecstatic.

Kalganov was well aware of Mitya's feelings for Grushenka, and he had guessed about the Pole too, but that didn't interest him much—perhaps didn't interest him at all. What he was interested in was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he had met the Poles here at the inn for the first time in his life. He already knew Grushenka and had once come with someone to see her, but she hadn't taken to him. Here, though, she was looking at him very affectionately: before Mitya's arrival, she had been making a fuss over him, but he seemed somehow unmoved by it. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick, fair hair. From his pale face looked out beautiful pale-blue eyes, with an intelligent and sometimes even deep expression, beyond his years—though the young man sometimes looked and talked quite like a child, and wasn't at all ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Sometimes there was something fixed and obstinate in his expression. He would look at you and listen, seeming all the while to be persistently dreaming about something else. Often he was listless and lazy; at other times he would grow excited, sometimes, apparently, over the most trivial matters.

“Just imagine, I've been taking him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling his words indolently, yet quite naturally, without the slightest affectation. “Ever since your brother, remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That made me take an interest in him at the time, and I brought him out to the country, but he keeps talking such rubbish I'm ashamed to be seen with him. I'm taking him back.”
“The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is impossible,” the Pole with the pipe remarked to Maximov.
He spoke Russian fairly well—much better, in any case, than he pretended. When he did use Russian words, he always twisted them into a Polish form.
“But I was married to a Polish lady myself,” Maximov tittered.
“But were you in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov put in at once.
“Was he a cavalry officer, indeed? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly and turning his inquiring eyes on each speaker in turn, as though there was no telling what he might hear.

“No, you see,” Maximov turned to him. “What I mean is that those pretty Polish ladies—when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans—when one of them dances a mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten, a little white one, and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother look on and allow it. They allow it—and the next day the Uhlan comes and offers her his hand. That's how it is—offers her his hand, heh heh!” Maximov ended, tittering.

“The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole in the chair suddenly growled, and crossed one leg over the other. Mitya's eye was caught by the Pole's huge greased boot, with its thick, dirty sole. The clothing of both Poles looked rather greasy.
“Well, now it's _lajdak_! What's he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly annoyed.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, what the gentleman saw in Poland were servant girls, not ladies of good family,” the Pole with the pipe observed to Grushenka.
“You can count on that,” the tall Pole snapped contemptuously.
“What now! Let him talk! People talk—why stop them? It makes things cheerful,” Grushenka said crossly.
“I'm not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig, with a long look at Grushenka, and then, falling into dignified silence, he sucked on his pipe again.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman spoke the truth.” Kalganov got excited again, as though it were a matter of great importance. “He's never been in Poland, so how can he talk about it? You weren't married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Smolensk Province. But a Uhlan had brought her to Russia before that—my future wife, I mean—with her mamma, her aunt, and another female relative with a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. But he didn't marry her, because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” cried Kalganov.
“Yes. They both deceived me a little at the time and hid it. I thought she was just skipping; she kept hopping along. I thought it was for fun.”
“She was so pleased she was going to marry you!” yelped Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

“Yes, so pleased. But it turned out to be a very different cause. Afterwards, once we were married, that very evening, after the wedding, she confessed, and very touchingly begged my forgiveness. ‘I jumped over a puddle once when I was a child,' she said, ‘and hurt my leg.' Heh heh!”
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter, almost falling onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

“Do you know, that's the truth, he's not lying this time,” Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya. “And do you know, he's been married twice—it's his first wife he's talking about. But his second wife, do you know, ran away and is still alive.”
“Is that possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov with an expression of utter astonishment.

“Yes. She ran away. I had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov modestly agreed, “with a _monsieur_. And what was worse, she'd had all my little property transferred to her beforehand. ‘You're an educated man,' she told me. ‘You can always make a living.' She settled my affairs like that. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.' Heh heh!”

“Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he's lying—and he often is—he's only doing it to entertain us all. There's no harm in that, is there? You know, I sometimes like him. He's terribly low, but it's natural to him, isn't it? Don't you think? Some people are low out of self-interest, but he's just like that by nature. Just imagine—he claims (he was arguing about it all day yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Remember, there's a landowner in it named Maximov, whom Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, remember, ‘for inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov while in a drunken state.' Would you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov, and that he was beaten! Now, can that be? Tchitchikov made his journey at the latest at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don't fit. He couldn't have been beaten then, could he?”
It was hard to imagine what Kalganov was so excited about, but his excitement was genuine. Mitya followed along without objecting.
“Well, but what if they did beat him!” he cried, laughing.
“It's not that they beat me exactly, but what I mean is—” Maximov put in.
“What do you mean? Either they beat you or they didn't.”
“What time is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, with a bored expression. The other shrugged his shoulders in reply. Neither of them had a watch.

“Why not talk? Let other people talk. Must other people be quiet just because you're bored?” Grushenka flew at him, clearly looking for a fight. Something seemed for the first time to flash across Mitya's mind. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
“_Pani_, I didn't oppose it. I didn't say anything.”
“All right then. Come on, tell us your story,” Grushenka called to Maximov. “Why is everyone silent?”

“There's nothing to tell, it's all so silly,” Maximov answered at once, with evident satisfaction, affecting a mincing tone. “Besides, all of that's allegory in Gogol, since he gave all the names a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name—he was called Shkvornev. Fenardi really was named Fenardi, only he wasn't Italian but Russian, and Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl with pretty little legs in tights, and she had a short little skirt with spangles, and she kept spinning round and round—only not for four hours, but just four minutes—and she bewitched everyone—”
“But what were you beaten for?” cried Kalganov.
“For Piron!” Maximov answered.
“What Piron?” cried Mitya.

“The famous French writer, Piron. We were all drinking then, a big party of us, in a tavern at that very fair. They'd invited me, and first of all I began quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny get-up!' And Boileau answers that he's going to a masquerade—meaning to the baths, heh heh! And they took it personally, so I hurried to recite another one, very sarcastic and well known to all educated people:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don't know your way to the sea!

They were even more offended and began cursing me in the most unseemly way for it. And as bad luck would have it, to set things right, I started telling a very cultivated anecdote about Piron—how he wasn't accepted into the French Academy, and how, in revenge, he wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me.”
“But what for? What for?”
“For my education. People can beat a man for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
“Enough! That's all stupid, I don't want to listen. I thought it would be amusing,” Grushenka cut them off abruptly.

Mitya started, and at once stopped laughing. The tall Pole rose to his feet and, with the haughty air of a man bored and out of his element, began pacing from corner to corner of the room, his hands behind his back.
“Ah, he can't sit still,” Grushenka said, looking at him contemptuously. Mitya began to feel anxious. He noticed, too, that the Pole on the sofa was looking at him with an irritated expression.
“_Panie!_” cried Mitya. “Let's drink! And the other _pan_ too! Let's drink.”
In a flash he pulled three glasses toward him and filled them with champagne.
“To Poland, _panovie_, I drink to your Poland!” cried Mitya.
“I shall be delighted, _panie_,” said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and affable condescension, and he took his glass.
“And the other _pan_, what's his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!” Mitya urged.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” put in the Pole on the sofa.
Pan Vrublevsky came up to the table, swaying as he walked.
“To Poland, _panovie_!” cried Mitya, raising his glass. “Hurrah!”
All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and poured out three more glasses.
“Now to Russia, _panovie_, and let us be brothers!”
“Pour some for us,” said Grushenka. “I'll drink to Russia too!”
“So will I,” said Kalganov.
“And I would, too—to Russia, the old grandmother!” Maximov tittered.
“All! All!” cried Mitya. “Trifon Borissovitch, more bottles!”
The other three bottles Mitya had brought with him were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted again. All drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka tossed off her whole glass at once. The Poles didn't touch theirs.
“What's this, _panovie_?” cried Mitya. “You won't drink it?”
Pan Vrublevsky took up the glass, raised it, and said in a resonant voice:
“To Russia as she was before 1772.”
“Now, that's better!” cried the other Pole, and they both emptied their glasses at once.
“You're fools, you _panovie_,” burst suddenly from Mitya.
“_Panie!_” shouted both Poles menacingly, turning on Mitya like a pair of roosters. Pan Vrublevsky was especially furious.
“Can a man help loving his own country?” he shouted.

“Silence! No quarreling! I won't have any quarreling!” cried Grushenka imperiously, and she stamped her foot on the floor. Her face glowed, her eyes shone. The glass she had just drunk was taking effect. Mitya was terribly alarmed.
“_Panovie_, forgive me! It was my fault, I'm sorry. Vrublevsky, _panie_ Vrublevsky, I'm sorry.”
“Hold your tongue, you, anyway! Sit down, you stupid man!” Grushenka scolded with angry annoyance.
Everyone sat down, all fell silent, looking at one another.
“Gentlemen, I was the cause of it all,” Mitya began again, unable to make anything of Grushenka's words. “Come, why are we sitting here? What shall we do—to amuse ourselves again?”
“Ah, this is certainly anything but amusing!” Kalganov mumbled lazily.
“Let's play faro again, the way we just did,” Maximov tittered suddenly.
“Faro? Splendid!” cried Mitya. “If only the _panovie_—”
“It's lite, _panovie_,” the Pole on the sofa responded, reluctantly.
“That's true,” Pan Vrublevsky agreed.
“Lite? What do you mean, ‘lite'?” Grushenka asked.
“Late, _pani_! ‘A late hour,' I mean,” the Pole on the sofa explained.

“It's always late with them. They can't do anything!” Grushenka almost shrieked in anger. “They're dull themselves, so they want others to be dull too. Before you came, Mitya, they were just as silent and kept turning up their noses at me.”
“My goddess!” cried the Pole on the sofa. “I see you're not well-disposed to me, and that's why I'm gloomy. I'm ready, _panie_,” he added, turning to Mitya.
“Begin, _panie_,” Mitya agreed, pulling his notes out of his pocket and laying two hundred-rouble notes on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take the cards. Make the bank.”
“We'll have cards from the landlord, _panie_,” said the little Pole gravely and emphatically.
“That's much the best way,” chimed in Pan Vrublevsky.
“From the landlord? Very well, I understand, let's get them from him. Cards!” Mitya shouted to the landlord.

The landlord brought in a new, unopened pack and informed Mitya that the girls were getting ready and that the Jews with the cymbals would likely be there soon, but the cart with the provisions hadn't yet arrived. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give orders, but only three girls had arrived, and Marya wasn't there yet. He didn't know himself what orders to give, or why he had run out. He only told them to take the presents for the girls out of the box—the sweets, the toffee, and the fondants. “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!” he cried hurriedly. “I was rude to Andrey!”
Suddenly Maximov, who had followed him out, touched him on the shoulder.
“Give me five roubles,” he whispered to Mitya. “I'll stake something at faro too, heh heh!”
“Capital! Splendid! Take ten, here!”
Again he took all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. “And if you lose that, come again, come again.”

“Very good,” Maximov whispered joyfully, and he hurried back again. Mitya too returned, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had already sat down and opened the pack. They looked much more amiable now, almost cordial. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was preparing to deal. He wore an air of solemnity.
“To your places, gentlemen,” cried Pan Vrublevsky.
“No, I'm not going to play any more,” Kalganov remarked. “I lost fifty roubles to them just now.”
“The _pan_ had no luck—perhaps he'll be lucky this time,” the Pole on the sofa said in his direction.
“How much is in the bank? To match?” asked Mitya.
“That's as you like, _panie_—maybe a hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you want to stake.”
“A million!” laughed Mitya.
“The Pan Captain has perhaps heard of Pan Podvysotsky?”
“What Podvysotsky?”

“In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone who came could stake against it. Podvysotsky comes in, sees a thousand gold pieces, and stakes against the bank. The banker says, ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky, are you laying down the gold, or must we trust to your honor?' ‘To my honor, _panie_,' says Podvysotsky. ‘So much the better.' The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. ‘Take it, _panie_,' says the banker, and pulling out the drawer, he hands him a million. ‘Take it, _panie_, these are your winnings.' There was a million in the bank. ‘I didn't know that,' says Podvysotsky. ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky,' said the banker, ‘you pledged your honor, and we pledged ours.' Podvysotsky took the million.”
“That's not true,” said Kalganov.
“_Panie_ Kalganov, in gentlemanly society one doesn't say such things.”

“As if a Polish gambler would give away a million!” cried Mitya, but he checked himself at once. “Forgive me, _panie_, it's my fault again—he would, he would give away a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I stake ten roubles—the knave leads.”

“And I'll put a rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little _panienotchka_, heh heh!” laughed Maximov, pulling out his queen and, as though trying to hide it from everyone, moved right up and crossed himself hurriedly under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won too.
“A corner!” cried Mitya.
“I'll bet another rouble, a ‘single' stake,” Maximov muttered gleefully, thrilled at having won a rouble.
“Lost!” shouted Mitya. “A ‘double' on the seven!”
The seven was trumped too.
“Stop!” cried Kalganov suddenly.
“Double! Double!” Mitya kept doubling his stakes, and each time he doubled, the card he doubled was trumped by the Poles. The rouble stakes kept winning.
“On the double!” shouted Mitya furiously.
“You've lost two hundred, _panie_. Will you stake another hundred?” asked the Pole on the sofa.
“What? Lost two hundred already? Then another two hundred! All on doubles!”
And pulling his money out of his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
“That's enough!” he shouted in his ringing voice.
“What's the matter?” Mitya stared at him.
“That's enough! I don't want you to play any more. Don't!”
“Why?”
“Because I don't. Damn it, come away. That's why. I won't let you go on playing.”
Mitya gazed at him in astonishment.
“Give it up, Mitya. He may be right. You've lost a lot already,” Grushenka said, with a strange note in her voice. Both Poles rose from their seats with a deeply offended air.
“Are you joking, _panie_?” said the short one, looking severely at Kalganov.
“How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov too.
“Don't you dare shout like that,” cried Grushenka. “Ah, you turkey-cocks!”
Mitya looked at each of them in turn. But something in Grushenka's face suddenly struck him, and at the same instant something new flashed into his mind—a strange new thought!
“_Pani_ Agrippina,” the little Pole was beginning, crimson with anger, when Mitya suddenly walked up to him and slapped him on the shoulder.
“Most illustrious, two words with you.”
“What do you want?”
“In the next room—I've two words to say to you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You'll be glad to hear it.”
The little _pan_ was taken aback and looked apprehensively at Mitya. He agreed at once, however, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky went with them.
“The bodyguard? Let him come—I want him there too. I must have him!” cried Mitya. “March, _panovie_!”
“Where are you going?” Grushenka asked anxiously.
“We'll be back in a moment,” Mitya answered.
There was a sort of boldness, a sudden confidence shining in his eyes. His face had looked very different when he entered the room an hour before.

He led the Poles not into the large room where the chorus of girls was assembling and the table was being set, but into the bedroom on the right, where the trunks and packages were kept, and where there were two large beds with pyramids of cotton pillows on each. A lighted candle stood on a small deal table in the corner. The small man and Mitya sat down at this table, facing each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood beside them, his hands behind his back. The Poles looked severe but were obviously curious.
“What can I do for you, _panie_?” lisped the little Pole.
“Well, look here, _panie_, I won't keep you long. There's money for you,” he said, pulling out his notes. “Would you like three thousand? Take it and go on your way.”
The Pole stared wide-eyed at Mitya, with a searching look.
“Three thousand, _panie_?” He exchanged glances with Vrublevsky.

“Three, _panovie_, three! Listen, _panie_, I see you're a sensible man. Take three thousand and go to the devil, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear? But at once, this very minute, and for good. You understand, _panie_—for good. Here's the door, you go out of it. What do you have there, an overcoat, a fur coat? I'll bring it out to you. They'll get the horses ready right away, and then—goodbye, _panie_!”
Mitya awaited an answer with assurance. He had no doubts. An expression of extraordinary resolution passed over the Pole's face.
“And the money, _panie_?”

“The money, _panie_? Five hundred roubles I'll give you this instant for the journey, as a first installment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow, in the town—I swear on my honor, I'll get it, I'll get it at any cost!” cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man's face looked more forbidding.

“Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, at once, this minute, cash in hand!” Mitya added, feeling something was wrong. “What's the matter, _panie_? Don't you trust me? I can't give you the whole three thousand straight off. If I did, you might come back to her tomorrow. Besides, I don't have the three thousand here. It's at home in the town,” Mitya faltered, his spirits sinking with every word. “I swear, the money's there, hidden.”
In an instant an extraordinary sense of personal dignity rose in the little man's face.
“What next?” he asked ironically. “For shame!” and he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
“You spit, _panie_,” said Mitya, recognizing in despair that it was all over, “because you hope to get more out of Grushenka? You're a pair of capons, that's what you are!”

“This is a mortal insult!” The little Pole turned as red as a crab and walked briskly out of the room, as though unwilling to hear another word. Vrublevsky stormed out after him, and Mitya followed, confused and crestfallen. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the _pan_ would at once raise an outcry. And that's exactly what he did. The Pole walked into the room and threw himself into a theatrical pose before Grushenka.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, I have received a mortal insult!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they had wounded her in the tenderest spot.
“Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she cried. “Not another word of Polish! You used to talk Russian. You can't have forgotten it in five years.”
She was red with passion.
“_Pani_ Agrippina—”
“My name's Agrafena, Grushenka—speak Russian, or I won't listen!”
The Pole gasped with offended dignity and, quickly and pompously, delivered himself in broken Russian:
“_Pani_ Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget everything that has happened up to today—”
“Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him short, jumping up from her seat.
“Just so, _pani_, I'm not pusillanimous, I'm magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya, in the other room, offered me three thousand to depart. I spat in the _pan's_ face.”
“What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterically. “Is it true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
“_Panie, panie!_” yelled Mitya. “She's pure and shining, and I have never been her lover! That's a lie—”

“How dare you defend me to him?” shrieked Grushenka. “It wasn't virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn't that I was afraid of Kuzma—I did it so I could hold my head up when I met him and tell him he's a scoundrel. And he actually refused the money?”
“He took it! He took it!” cried Mitya. “Only he wanted the whole three thousand at once, and I could only give him seven hundred straight off.”
“I see: he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!”
“_Pani_ Agrippina!” cried the little Pole. “I'm a knight, I'm a nobleman, and not a _lajdak_. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman—perverse and shameless.”

“Oh, go back where you came from! I'll tell them to throw you out, and you'll be thrown out,” cried Grushenka, furious. “I've been a fool, a fool, to have been miserable these five years! And it wasn't for his sake—it was my anger that made me miserable. And this isn't him at all! Was he like this? This could be his father! Where did you get your wig from? He was a falcon, but this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing to me. And I've been crying for five years, damned fool, abject, shameless that I was!”
She sank back in her low chair and hid her face in her hands. At that instant the chorus of Mokroe began singing in the room on the left—a rollicking dance song.
“A regular Sodom!” Vrublevsky roared suddenly. “Landlord, send the shameless hussies away!”
The landlord, who had been curiously peeping in at the door for some time, heard the shouts and, guessing that his guests were quarreling, entered the room at once.
“What are you shouting for? You want to split your throat?” he said to Vrublevsky with surprising rudeness.
“Animal!” bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

“Animal? And what sort of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You played with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, do you know that? It's the same as false banknotes—”
And going up to the sofa, he thrust his fingers between the back of the sofa and the cushion and pulled out an unopened pack of cards.
“Here's my pack, unopened!”
He held it up and showed it to everyone in the room. “From where I stood, I saw him slip my pack away and put his in place of it—you're a cheat, not a gentleman!”
“And I saw the _pan_ change a card twice!” cried Kalganov.
“How shameful! How shameful!” exclaimed Grushenka, clasping her hands and blushing with genuine shame. “Good Lord, he's come to that!”
“I thought so too!” said Mitya. But before he had finished the words, Vrublevsky, with a confused and infuriated face, shook his fist at Grushenka, shouting:
“You low harlot!”
Mitya flew at him at once, seized him with both hands, lifted him into the air, and in an instant had carried him into the room on the right, from which they had just come.
“I've laid him on the floor in there,” he announced, returning at once, gasping with excitement. “He's struggling, the scoundrel! But he won't come back, no fear of that!”
He closed one half of the folding doors and, holding the other ajar, called out to the little Pole:
“Most illustrious, will you be pleased to retire as well?”
“My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch, “make them give you back the money you lost. It's as good as stolen from you.”
“I don't want my fifty roubles back,” Kalganov declared suddenly.
“I don't want my two hundred either,” cried Mitya. “I wouldn't take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation.”
“Bravo, Mitya! You're a trump, Mitya!” cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in her exclamation.
The little _pan_, crimson with fury but still mindful of his dignity, was making for the door, but he stopped short and said suddenly, addressing Grushenka:
“_Pani_, if you want to come with me, come. If not, goodbye.”

And swelling with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. This was a man of character: he had so high an opinion of himself that after all that had happened, he still expected her to marry him. Mitya slammed the door after him.
“Lock it,” said Kalganov. But the key clicked on the other side—they had locked it from within.
“That's capital!” exclaimed Grushenka relentlessly. “Serves them right!”
